spec.description: Solid lower-right triangular half of a square, with dashed left and top square edges and a right-angle marker at bottom right.
spec.mathematics: A unit square is bisected by its bottom-left to top-right diagonal.
spec.answerVisibility: No side lengths or acute-angle answers are supplied.

answer.short: Bottom and right sides: $1$ each. Diagonal: $\sqrt2$. Acute angles: $45^\circ$ each; bottom-right angle: $90^\circ$.
answer.worked:
The two perpendicular sides each have length $1$. By Pythagoras’ theorem,
$$\begin{aligned}h^2&=1^2+1^2\\h&=\sqrt2.\end{aligned}$$
The triangle is isosceles, so each acute angle is $(180^\circ-90^\circ)\div2=45^\circ$.

spec.description: Complete labelled version of the unit-square construction.
spec.mathematics: Legs 1 and 1, hypotenuse square root of 2, acute angles 45 degrees.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Label the sides and angles of the triangle.

spec.description: Upright equilateral triangle bisected by a solid vertical altitude. Left sloping edge and left half-base are dashed; right half is solid.
spec.mathematics: The altitude bisects the unit equilateral triangle into two congruent right triangles.
spec.answerVisibility: No lengths or acute-angle labels are supplied.

answer.short: Right-hand triangle: hypotenuse $1$, base $\frac12$, altitude $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$; apex angle $30^\circ$, bottom-right angle $60^\circ$, foot angle $90^\circ$.
answer.worked:
The altitude bisects the base and the apex angle. The half-base is $\frac12$, the apex angle is $30^\circ$, and the bottom-right angle is $60^\circ$. By Pythagoras’ theorem,
$$\begin{aligned}h^2+\left(\frac12\right)^2&=1^2\\h^2&=\frac34\\h&=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.\end{aligned}$$

inlines.text: Consider a right-angled triangle as its two acute angles approach
A triangle doesn’t exist when an angle is 0°; we are finding the values of the ratios.

spec.description: Very shallow right triangle with left tip, horizontal base, short right vertical edge and bottom-right right-angle marker. It illustrates an approach to degeneracy, not a triangle with an actual zero angle.
spec.mathematics: The acute angles approach 0 and 90 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: No numerical labels or answers are supplied.

answer.worked:
As the smaller angle approaches $0^\circ$, the opposite side approaches zero and the adjacent side approaches the hypotenuse. The sine and cosine values extend to $\sin0^\circ=0$, $\cos0^\circ=1$, $\sin90^\circ=1$ and $\cos90^\circ=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}\tan0^\circ&=\frac01=0.\end{aligned}$$
At $90^\circ$, the tangent ratio would require division by zero, so $\tan90^\circ$ is undefined.

teachingContext.methodNote: The preceding investigation derives exact ratios using a halved unit square and a halved unit equilateral triangle, then considers the endpoint angles. This supplied table summarises those values for memorisation.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the standard exact trigonometric values in a supplied table.

answer.worked:
For $45^\circ$, the unit-square triangle has legs $1,1$ and hypotenuse $\sqrt2$, so $\sin45^\circ=\cos45^\circ=\frac1{\sqrt2}$ and $\tan45^\circ=1$.

Halving a unit equilateral triangle gives hypotenuse $1$, shorter leg $\frac12$ and longer leg $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$. Hence $\sin30^\circ=\cos60^\circ=\frac12$, $\cos30^\circ=\sin60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, $\tan30^\circ=\frac1{\sqrt3}$ and $\tan60^\circ=\sqrt3$.

The endpoint values are $\sin0^\circ=0$, $\cos0^\circ=1$, $\tan0^\circ=0$, $\sin90^\circ=1$ and $\cos90^\circ=0$. Since $\cos90^\circ=0$, $\tan90^\circ$ is undefined.

spec.description: Triangle with horizontal base and upper apex; left side 6, right side x, base angles 60 degrees at left and 45 degrees at right.
spec.mathematics: The side 6 is opposite 45 degrees; x is opposite 60 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied side and angle labels are visible.

answer.worked:
Draw a perpendicular from the apex to the base and let its length be $h$.

$$\begin{align*}\sin60^\circ&=\frac{h}{6}\\h&=6\times\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\h&=3\sqrt3\\\sin45^\circ&=\frac{3\sqrt3}{x}\\x&=\frac{3\sqrt3}{1/\sqrt2}\\x&=3\sqrt6\end{align*}$$

spec.answerVisibility: No altitude, half-base length or calculated height is supplied.

answer.worked:
Draw the altitude from the apex to the base. It bisects the base and forms two right triangles, each with hypotenuse $4$ and a $60^{\circ}$ base angle.
$$\begin{align*}\sin60^{\circ}&=\frac{x}{4}\\x&=4\times\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\x&=2\sqrt3\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Nested right triangles share base 9 and a vertical left side. The upper segment of the left side is x. At the right vertex, the base-to-inner-slope angle is 30 degrees and the angle between slopes is 15 degrees, labelled by an external leader.
spec.mathematics: The outer right triangle has a 45-degree angle at the right vertex. The required length is its height minus the inner triangle's height.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and x are visible; the derived 45-degree angle and heights are omitted.

answer.worked:
The angle between the base and the upper sloping side is $30^{\circ}+15^{\circ}=45^{\circ}$. Let $H$ be the whole vertical height and $h$ the lower vertical height.
$$\begin{align*}H&=9\tan45^{\circ}\\H&=9\\h&=9\tan30^{\circ}\\h&=\frac{9}{\sqrt3}=3\sqrt3\\x&=H-h\\x&=9-3\sqrt3\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Two right triangles share a vertical side of length 20. Their sloping sides meet the baseline at distinct points with angles 45 degrees and 30 degrees. A dimension arrow beneath the baseline marks the interval x between those points.
spec.mathematics: The inner baseline length is 20/tan45 degrees; the outer baseline length is 20/tan30 degrees. Their difference is x.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and x are visible.

answer.worked:
Let $L$ be the whole baseline length and $l$ the shorter baseline length.
$$\begin{align*}\tan30^{\circ}&=\frac{20}{L}\\L&=\frac{20}{\tan30^{\circ}}=20\sqrt3\\\tan45^{\circ}&=\frac{20}{l}\\l&=\frac{20}{\tan45^{\circ}}=20\\x&=L-l\\x&=20\sqrt3-20\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: For this question, use the identity $\cos 2\theta=1-2\sin^{2}\theta$.

answer.worked:
Let $\theta=15^{\circ}$.
$$\begin{align*}\cos30^{\circ}&=1-2\sin^{2}15^{\circ}\\\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&=1-2s^{2}\\2s^{2}&=1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\2s^{2}&=\frac{2-\sqrt3}{2}\\s^{2}&=\frac{2-\sqrt3}{4}\\s&=\frac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt3}}{2}\end{align*}$$
Take the positive root because $\sin15^{\circ}>0$.

Using parts a and b,
$$\begin{align*}s^{2}&=\frac{2-\sqrt3}{4}\\s^{2}&=\frac{\dfrac{(\sqrt3-1)^{2}}{2}}{4}\\s^{2}&=\frac{(\sqrt3-1)^{2}}{8}\\s&=\frac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt8}\\s&=\frac{\sqrt3-1}{2\sqrt2}\end{align*}$$
Since $s=\sin15^{\circ}>0$ and $\sqrt3-1>0$, take the positive root. Thus $\sin15^{\circ}=\dfrac{\sqrt3-1}{2\sqrt2}$.

spec.description: Unshaded triangle PRS with Q between P and R, internal segment QS, and a right-angle marker at R.
spec.mathematics: P, Q and R are collinear in that order. SR is perpendicular to PR. Angle SPR is 15 degrees and angle SQR is 30 degrees. Coordinates derive these relationships; no numerical side lengths are printed.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied vertex labels, angle values and right-angle marker are visible.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle PQS&=180^{\circ}-30^{\circ}\\&=150^{\circ}\\\angle PSQ&=180^{\circ}-150^{\circ}-15^{\circ}\\&=15^{\circ}\end{align*}$$
The first calculation uses angles on a straight line. Since $\angle PSQ=\angle QPS$, the opposite sides are equal. Hence $PQ=QS$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Given that the length of $SR$ is 1 unit, write the lengths of $QR$, $QS$, and $PQ$.

answer.worked:
In right-angled triangle $QRS$,
$$\begin{align*}\sin30^{\circ}&=\frac{SR}{QS}\\\frac12&=\frac1{QS}\\QS&=2\end{align*}$$
By part a, $PQ=QS=2$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan30^{\circ}&=\frac{SR}{QR}\\\frac1{\sqrt3}&=\frac1{QR}\\QR&=\sqrt3\end{align*}$$
Thus $QR=\sqrt3$ units and $QS=PQ=2$ units.

content.prompt: For this question, use the identity $\tan 2\theta=\dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^2\theta}$.

answer.worked:
Cross multiply the result from part a.
$$\begin{align*}2\sqrt3t&=1-t^2\\t^2+2\sqrt3t-1&=0.\end{align*}$$

Using the quadratic formula,
$$\begin{align*}t&=\frac{-2\sqrt3\pm\sqrt{12+4}}{2}\\t&=-\sqrt3\pm2.\end{align*}$$
Since $t=\tan15^\circ>0$, reject $-\sqrt3-2$.
$$\tan15^\circ=2-\sqrt3.$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Use a similar technique to find the exact value for $\tan22.5^\circ$.

answer.worked:
Let $u=\tan22.5^\circ$ and substitute $\theta=22.5^\circ$ into the identity.
$$\begin{align*}\tan45^\circ&=\frac{2u}{1-u^2}\\1&=\frac{2u}{1-u^2}\\1-u^2&=2u\\u^2+2u-1&=0\\u&=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{4+4}}{2}\\u&=-1\pm\sqrt2.\end{align*}$$
Since $\tan22.5^\circ>0$, reject $-1-\sqrt2$.
$$\tan22.5^\circ=\sqrt2-1.$$

answer.worked:
For angle $x$, the opposite side is $a$ and the hypotenuse is $b$.
$$\sin x=\frac{a}{b}$$

For angle $x$, the adjacent side is $c$ and the hypotenuse is $b$.
$$\cos x=\frac{c}{b}$$

For angle $x$, the opposite side is $a$ and the adjacent side is $c$.
$$\tan x=\frac{a}{c}$$

For angle $90^{\circ}-x$, the opposite side is $c$ and the hypotenuse is $b$.
$$\sin(90^{\circ}-x)=\frac{c}{b}$$

For angle $90^{\circ}-x$, the adjacent side is $a$ and the hypotenuse is $b$.
$$\cos(90^{\circ}-x)=\frac{a}{b}$$

For angle $90^{\circ}-x$, the opposite side is $c$ and the adjacent side is $a$.
$$\tan(90^{\circ}-x)=\frac{c}{a}$$

content.prompt: Convert these true bearings to angles of inclination.

answer.worked:
The direction is $70^{\circ}$ clockwise from north, so it is above the positive $x$-axis.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=90^{\circ}-70^{\circ}\\\theta&=20^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

A bearing of $180^{\circ}$ points south. Measure anticlockwise from the positive $x$-axis to south.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=360^{\circ}-90^{\circ}\\\theta&=270^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

The direction is northwest, $45^{\circ}$ anticlockwise from north.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=360^{\circ}-315^{\circ}\\\alpha&=45^{\circ}\\\theta&=90^{\circ}+45^{\circ}\\\theta&=135^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
Add or subtract $360^{\circ}$ repeatedly:
$$\begin{aligned}30^{\circ}+360^{\circ}&=390^{\circ}\\390^{\circ}+360^{\circ}&=750^{\circ}\\30^{\circ}-360^{\circ}&=-330^{\circ}\\-330^{\circ}-360^{\circ}&=-690^{\circ}\\-690^{\circ}-360^{\circ}&=-1050^{\circ}.\end{aligned}$$
Together with $30^{\circ}$, these give six possible angles. In general, $\theta=30^{\circ}+360^{\circ}n$, where $n$ is an integer.

The terminal ray is in quadrant II, where sine is positive. The reference angle is $180^\circ-150^\circ=30^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned}\sin150^\circ&=\sin30^\circ\\&=\frac12\end{aligned}$$

The terminal ray is in quadrant III, where sine is negative. The reference angle is $225^\circ-180^\circ=45^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned}\sin225^\circ&=-\sin45^\circ\\&=-\frac1{\sqrt2}\end{aligned}$$

The terminal ray is in quadrant IV, where cosine is positive. The reference angle is $360^\circ-300^\circ=60^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned}\cos300^\circ&=\cos60^\circ\\&=\frac12\end{aligned}$$

The terminal ray is in quadrant II, where cosine is negative. The reference angle is $180^\circ-150^\circ=30^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned}\cos150^\circ&=-\cos30^\circ\\&=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\end{aligned}$$

The terminal ray is in quadrant IV, where cosine is positive. The reference angle is $360^\circ-300^\circ=60^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned}\cos300^\circ&=\cos60^\circ\\&=\frac12\end{aligned}$$

The terminal ray is in quadrant IV, where tangent is negative. The reference angle is $360^\circ-300^\circ=60^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned}\tan300^\circ&=-\tan60^\circ\\&=-\sqrt3\end{aligned}$$

The terminal ray is in quadrant II, where tangent is negative. The reference angle is $180^\circ-135^\circ=45^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned}\tan135^\circ&=-\tan45^\circ\\&=-1\end{aligned}$$

The terminal ray is in quadrant III, where tangent is positive. The reference angle is $240^\circ-180^\circ=60^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned}\tan240^\circ&=\tan60^\circ\\&=\sqrt3\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt:
The points $P,Q,R,S$ are on the unit circle. $A(1,0)$ and $O$ is the origin. Find the exact coordinates of $P,Q,R,S$ if:

$\angle AOP=60^{\circ}$, $\angle AOQ=120^{\circ}$, $\angle AOR=240^{\circ}$, $\angle AOS=30^{\circ}$.

spec.description: Unit circle with positive axis arrowheads, radii to four marked points, labels P, Q, R, S and A, and numeric labels 1 and −1. The Cartesian-origin O label is omitted under the graph convention.
spec.mathematics: P is at 60°, Q at 120°, R at 240° and S at 330°. S lies 30° clockwise from OA.
spec.answerVisibility: Question figure contains point locations and names, but no coordinate answers.

answer.worked:
On the unit circle, $(x,y)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$. The diagram places $S$ in quadrant IV, so its directed angle is $330^{\circ}$.

$\begin{aligned}P&=(\cos60^{\circ},\sin60^{\circ})\\&=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\\Q&=(-\cos60^{\circ},\sin60^{\circ})\\&=\left(-\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\\R&=(-\cos60^{\circ},-\sin60^{\circ})\\&=\left(-\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\\S&=(\cos30^{\circ},-\sin30^{\circ})\\&=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2},-\frac12\right)\end{aligned}$

content.prompt: Use the trigonometric graphs to find the values (if they exist) of these trigonometric ratios of boundary angles.

answer.worked: The sine graph passes through $(0^{\circ},0)$, so $\sin 0^{\circ}=0$.
At $180^{\circ}$, the cosine graph has height $-1$, so $\cos 180^{\circ}=-1$.
The cosine graph crosses the horizontal axis at $90^{\circ}$, so $\cos 90^{\circ}=0$.
The tangent graph passes through $(0^{\circ},0)$, so $\tan 0^{\circ}=0$.
At $90^{\circ}$, the sine graph has height $1$, so $\sin 90^{\circ}=1$.
At $0^{\circ}$, the cosine graph has height $1$, so $\cos 0^{\circ}=1$.
At $270^{\circ}$, the sine graph has height $-1$, so $\sin 270^{\circ}=-1$.
The cosine graph crosses the horizontal axis at $270^{\circ}$, so $\cos 270^{\circ}=0$.
The sine graph crosses the horizontal axis at $180^{\circ}$, so $\sin 180^{\circ}=0$.
The tangent graph has no point at $270^{\circ}$; its branches approach a vertical asymptote there. Thus $\tan 270^{\circ}$ is undefined.
The tangent graph has no point at $90^{\circ}$; its branches approach a vertical asymptote there. Thus $\tan 90^{\circ}$ is undefined.
The tangent graph crosses the horizontal axis at $180^{\circ}$, so $\tan 180^{\circ}=0$.

answer.worked: On the sine graph, the ordinate at $60^{\circ}$ is positive and the ordinate at $200^{\circ}$ is negative. Hence $\sin60^{\circ}>\sin200^{\circ}$.
The sine graph is above the axis at $100^{\circ}$ and below it at $300^{\circ}$. Thus $\sin100^{\circ}>\sin300^{\circ}$.
On the sine graph, the ordinate at $135^{\circ}$ is higher than the ordinate at $10^{\circ}$. Thus $\sin135^{\circ}>\sin10^{\circ}$.
The sine graph has the same ordinate at $200^{\circ}$ and $340^{\circ}$, so $\sin200^{\circ}=\sin340^{\circ}$.
The cosine graph is positive at $70^{\circ}$ and negative at $125^{\circ}$. Thus $\cos70^{\circ}>\cos125^{\circ}$.
The cosine graph is positive at $315^{\circ}$ and negative at $135^{\circ}$. Hence $\cos315^{\circ}>\cos135^{\circ}$.
The cosine graph has the same ordinate at $310^{\circ}$ and $50^{\circ}$. Hence $\cos310^{\circ}=\cos50^{\circ}$.
Both ordinates are negative, but the cosine graph at $95^{\circ}$ is closer to zero and higher than at $260^{\circ}$. Hence $\cos95^{\circ}>\cos260^{\circ}$.
The sine graph at $90^{\circ}$ and the cosine graph at $360^{\circ}$ both have ordinate $1$.
At $180^{\circ}$, the cosine graph has ordinate $-1$ and the sine graph has ordinate $0$. These values are unequal.
The sine graph at $210^{\circ}$ has ordinate $-0.5$, which is higher than its ordinate near $-1$ at $285^{\circ}$. Hence $\sin210^{\circ}>\sin285^{\circ}$.
The cosine graph is positive at $15^{\circ}$ and negative at $115^{\circ}$. Hence $\cos15^{\circ}>\cos115^{\circ}$.

content.prompt: $f(x)=\sin x+\cos(90^{\circ}-x)$. Decide whether $f(x)$ is odd, even, or neither.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\sin x+\sin x\\f(x)&=2\sin x\\f(-x)&=2\sin(-x)\\f(-x)&=-2\sin x\\f(-x)&=-f(x)\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $f$ is odd.

content.prompt: $g(x)=x\sin(-x)+\cos(-x)$. Decide whether $g(x)$ is odd, even, or neither.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}g(x)&=-x\sin x+\cos x\\g(-x)&=-(-x)\sin(-x)+\cos(-x)\\g(-x)&=-x\sin x+\cos x\\g(-x)&=g(x)\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $g$ is even.

content.prompt: $f(x)=x^2\sin(-x)+x\cos(-x)$. Decide whether $f(x)$ is odd, even, or neither.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f(x)&=-x^2\sin x+x\cos x\\f(-x)&=-(-x)^2\sin(-x)+(-x)\cos(-x)\\f(-x)&=x^2\sin x-x\cos x\\f(-x)&=-f(x)\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $f$ is odd.

content.prompt:
These equations have solutions at boundary angles, i.e. on the edges of the quadrants.

We solve these using the graphs, a diagram of the unit circle, or knowledge of exact values.

Solve for $0\le\theta<360^{\circ}$.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 3, shared figure at lower right

answer.worked: Sine is the $y$-coordinate. The point with $y=1$ is $(0,1)$, so $\theta=90^{\circ}$.
Cosine is the $x$-coordinate. The point with $x=1$ is $(1,0)$, so $\theta=0^{\circ}$. The endpoint $360^{\circ}$ is excluded.
$\tan\theta=\frac{y}{x}=0$ when $y=0$ and $x\ne0$. The points $(1,0)$ and $(-1,0)$ give $\theta=0^{\circ}$ or $180^{\circ}$. The endpoint $360^{\circ}$ is excluded.
Sine is the $y$-coordinate. The point with $y=-1$ is $(0,-1)$, so $\theta=270^{\circ}$.
Cosine is the $x$-coordinate. The points with $x=0$ are $(0,1)$ and $(0,-1)$, so $\theta=90^{\circ}$ or $270^{\circ}$.
Sine is the $y$-coordinate. The points with $y=0$ are $(1,0)$ and $(-1,0)$, so $\theta=0^{\circ}$ or $180^{\circ}$. The endpoint $360^{\circ}$ is excluded.

content.prompt: Solve for $\theta\in[0^{\circ},360^{\circ})$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2\sin\theta-1&=0\\2\sin\theta&=1\\\sin\theta&=\frac12\\A&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)=30^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$
Sine is positive in Q1 and Q2.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=30^{\circ}\quad\text{or}\quad180^{\circ}-30^{\circ}\\\theta&=30^{\circ}\quad\text{or}\quad150^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\sqrt2\cos\theta-1&=0\\\sqrt2\cos\theta&=1\\\cos\theta&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\\A&=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)=45^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$
Cosine is positive in Q1 and Q4.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=45^{\circ}\quad\text{or}\quad360^{\circ}-45^{\circ}\\\theta&=45^{\circ}\quad\text{or}\quad315^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\sqrt3\tan\theta-2&=-1\\\sqrt3\tan\theta&=1\\\tan\theta&=\frac1{\sqrt3}\\A&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)=30^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$
Tangent is positive in Q1 and Q3.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=30^{\circ}\quad\text{or}\quad180^{\circ}+30^{\circ}\\\theta&=30^{\circ}\quad\text{or}\quad210^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}2\cos\theta+\sqrt3&=0\\2\cos\theta&=-\sqrt3\\\cos\theta&=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\A&=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=30^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$
Cosine is negative in Q2 and Q3.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=180^{\circ}-30^{\circ}\quad\text{or}\quad180^{\circ}+30^{\circ}\\\theta&=150^{\circ}\quad\text{or}\quad210^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}6\sin\theta+3&=0\\6\sin\theta&=-3\\\sin\theta&=-\frac12\\A&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)=30^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$
Sine is negative in Q3 and Q4.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=180^{\circ}+30^{\circ}\quad\text{or}\quad360^{\circ}-30^{\circ}\\\theta&=210^{\circ}\quad\text{or}\quad330^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}1+\tan\theta&=0\\\tan\theta&=-1\\A&=\tan^{-1}(1)=45^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$
Tangent is negative in Q2 and Q4.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=180^{\circ}-45^{\circ}\quad\text{or}\quad360^{\circ}-45^{\circ}\\\theta&=135^{\circ}\quad\text{or}\quad315^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Solve for $\theta\in[0^{\circ},360^{\circ})$. Remember to take positive and negative values when square rooting.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\sin\theta&=\pm\sqrt{1}\\\sin\theta&=\pm1\end{align*}$$
These values occur on the vertical axis of the unit circle.
$$\theta=90^{\circ},\ 270^{\circ}.$$

$$\begin{align*}\cos\theta&=\pm\sqrt{\frac34}\\\cos\theta&=\pm\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\A&=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\\A&=30^{\circ}\end{align*}$$
Both signs are included, so use all four quadrants.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=30^{\circ},\ 180^{\circ}-30^{\circ},\\&\phantom{=}180^{\circ}+30^{\circ},\ 360^{\circ}-30^{\circ}\\\theta&=30^{\circ},\ 150^{\circ},\ 210^{\circ},\ 330^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\pm\sqrt3\\A&=\tan^{-1}(\sqrt3)\\A&=60^{\circ}\end{align*}$$
Both signs are included, so use all four quadrants.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=60^{\circ},\ 180^{\circ}-60^{\circ},\\&\phantom{=}180^{\circ}+60^{\circ},\ 360^{\circ}-60^{\circ}\\\theta&=60^{\circ},\ 120^{\circ},\ 240^{\circ},\ 300^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Solve for $\theta\in[0^{\circ},360^{\circ})$. Remember, to solve quadratic equations we need to factorise.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta&=0\\\cos\theta(2\cos\theta-1)&=0\\\cos\theta&=0\quad\text{or}\quad\cos\theta=\frac12.\end{align*}$$
For $\cos\theta=0$, $\theta=90^{\circ},270^{\circ}$.
For $\cos\theta=\frac12$, $A=\cos^{-1}(\frac12)=60^{\circ}$. Cosine is positive in Q1 and Q4, so $\theta=60^{\circ},300^{\circ}$.
Hence $\theta=60^{\circ},90^{\circ},270^{\circ},300^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}\tan^2\theta-\tan\theta&=0\\\tan\theta(\tan\theta-1)&=0\\\tan\theta&=0\quad\text{or}\quad\tan\theta=1.\end{align*}$$
For $\tan\theta=0$, $\theta=0^{\circ},180^{\circ}$.
For $\tan\theta=1$, $A=\tan^{-1}(1)=45^{\circ}$. Tangent is positive in Q1 and Q3, so $\theta=45^{\circ},225^{\circ}$.
Hence $\theta=0^{\circ},45^{\circ},180^{\circ},225^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}2\cos^2\theta-1&=0\\(\sqrt2\cos\theta-1)(\sqrt2\cos\theta+1)&=0\\\cos\theta&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\quad\text{or}\quad\cos\theta=-\frac1{\sqrt2}.\end{align*}$$
$A=\cos^{-1}(\frac1{\sqrt2})=45^{\circ}$. The positive and negative ratios give solutions in all four quadrants.
$\theta=45^{\circ},135^{\circ},225^{\circ},315^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}3\tan^2\theta-1&=0\\(\sqrt3\tan\theta-1)(\sqrt3\tan\theta+1)&=0\\\tan\theta&=\frac1{\sqrt3}\quad\text{or}\quad\tan\theta=-\frac1{\sqrt3}.\end{align*}$$
$A=\tan^{-1}(\frac1{\sqrt3})=30^{\circ}$. The positive and negative ratios give solutions in all four quadrants.
$\theta=30^{\circ},150^{\circ},210^{\circ},330^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}2\sin\theta-1&=0\quad\text{or}\quad\sin\theta+1=0\\\sin\theta&=\frac12\quad\text{or}\quad\sin\theta=-1.\end{align*}$$
For $\sin\theta=\frac12$, $A=\sin^{-1}(\frac12)=30^{\circ}$. Sine is positive in Q1 and Q2, so $\theta=30^{\circ},150^{\circ}$.
For $\sin\theta=-1$, $\theta=270^{\circ}$.
Hence $\theta=30^{\circ},150^{\circ},270^{\circ}$.

content.prompt: Jimmy solved $\tan^2\theta=\tan\theta$ for $\theta\in[0^\circ,360^\circ)$ by dividing both sides by $\tan\theta$ first. He got the solutions $45^\circ$ and $225^\circ$, which are not all the solutions.

answer.short: Dividing by $\tan\theta$ assumes $\tan\theta\ne0$, losing $\theta=0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$. Move all terms to the left, factorise and use the null factor law.
answer.worked:
Dividing by $\tan\theta$ excludes the case $\tan\theta=0$. Instead,
$$\begin{align*}\tan^2\theta-\tan\theta&=0\\\tan\theta(\tan\theta-1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $\tan\theta=0$ or $\tan\theta=1$.

For $\tan\theta=0$, $\theta=0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$.

For $\tan\theta=1$, the reference angle is $45^\circ$ and tangent is positive in Q1 and Q3, giving $\theta=45^\circ$ or $225^\circ$.

All solutions are $0^\circ,45^\circ,180^\circ,225^\circ$; Jimmy missed $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$.

content.prompt: Solve for $\theta\in[0^\circ,360^\circ)$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2\sin^2\theta-3\sin\theta+1&=0\\(2\sin\theta-1)(\sin\theta-1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$ or $\sin\theta=1$.

For $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$, $A=\sin^{-1}(\tfrac12)=30^\circ$. Sine is positive in Q1 and Q2, so $\theta=30^\circ$ or $180^\circ-30^\circ=150^\circ$.

For $\sin\theta=1$, $\theta=90^\circ$.

Thus $\theta=30^\circ,90^\circ,150^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta-3&=0\\(2\cos\theta-3)(\cos\theta+1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $\cos\theta=\tfrac32$ or $\cos\theta=-1$.

Since $-1\le\cos\theta\le1$, $\cos\theta=\tfrac32$ has no solution.

For $\cos\theta=-1$, $\theta=180^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta&=0\\\cos\theta(2\cos\theta-1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $\cos\theta=0$ or $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$.

For $\cos\theta=0$, $\theta=90^\circ$ or $270^\circ$.

For $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$, $A=\cos^{-1}(\tfrac12)=60^\circ$. Cosine is positive in Q1 and Q4, so $\theta=60^\circ$ or $360^\circ-60^\circ=300^\circ$.

Thus $\theta=60^\circ,90^\circ,270^\circ,300^\circ$.

The denominators require $\cos\theta\ne0$. Multiplying by $\cos^2\theta$ gives
$$\begin{align*}1+\cos\theta-2\cos^2\theta&=0\\2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta-1&=0\\(2\cos\theta+1)(\cos\theta-1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $\cos\theta=-\tfrac12$ or $\cos\theta=1$.

For $\cos\theta=-\tfrac12$, $A=\cos^{-1}(\tfrac12)=60^\circ$. Cosine is negative in Q2 and Q3, giving $\theta=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$ or $180^\circ+60^\circ=240^\circ$.

For $\cos\theta=1$, $\theta=0^\circ$ in the stated domain. The endpoint $360^\circ$ is excluded.

Thus $\theta=0^\circ,120^\circ,240^\circ$.

content.prompt: Solve for $\theta\in[0^{\circ},360^{\circ})$. Answer to the nearest minute where necessary.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2\sin\theta\cos\theta-\sin\theta&=0\\\sin\theta(2\cos\theta-1)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\sin\theta=0$ or $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$.
For $\sin\theta=0$, $\theta=0^{\circ},180^{\circ}$.
For $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$, the reference angle is $60^{\circ}$ and cosine is positive in Q1 and Q4, giving $\theta=60^{\circ},300^{\circ}$.
Thus $\theta=0^{\circ},60^{\circ},180^{\circ},300^{\circ}$. The upper endpoint $360^{\circ}$ is excluded.

$$\begin{align*}2\sin^2\theta+\sin\theta-1&=0\\(2\sin\theta-1)(\sin\theta+1)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$ or $\sin\theta=-1$.
For $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$, the reference angle is $30^{\circ}$ and sine is positive in Q1 and Q2, giving $\theta=30^{\circ},150^{\circ}$.
For $\sin\theta=-1$, $\theta=270^{\circ}$.
Thus $\theta=30^{\circ},150^{\circ},270^{\circ}$.

Since the denominators require $\cos\theta\ne0$, multiply by $\cos^2\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}1+2\cos\theta&=8\cos^2\theta\\8\cos^2\theta-2\cos\theta-1&=0\\(4\cos\theta+1)(2\cos\theta-1)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\cos\theta=-\tfrac14$ or $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$.
For $\cos\theta=-\tfrac14$, use the positive ratio:
$$A=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac14\right).$$
Cosine is negative in Q2 and Q3, so $\theta=180^{\circ}-A,180^{\circ}+A$, giving $104^{\circ}29',255^{\circ}31'$ to the nearest minute.
For $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$, $\theta=60^{\circ},300^{\circ}$.
Thus $\theta=60^{\circ},104^{\circ}29',255^{\circ}31',300^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}3\cos^2\theta+5\cos\theta-2&=0\\(3\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+2)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\cos\theta=\tfrac13$ or $\cos\theta=-2$. Reject $-2$ because $-1\le\cos\theta\le1$.
$$A=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac13\right).$$
Cosine is positive in Q1 and Q4, so $\theta=A,360^{\circ}-A$.
To the nearest minute, $\theta=70^{\circ}32',289^{\circ}28'$.

Since the denominators require $\sin\theta\ne0$, multiply by $\sin^2\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}4-4\sin\theta-15\sin^2\theta&=0\\15\sin^2\theta+4\sin\theta-4&=0\\(5\sin\theta-2)(3\sin\theta+2)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\sin\theta=\tfrac25$ or $\sin\theta=-\tfrac23$.
For $\sin\theta=\tfrac25$, let $A=\sin^{-1}(\tfrac25)$. Sine is positive in Q1 and Q2, so $\theta=A,180^{\circ}-A$, giving $23^{\circ}35',156^{\circ}25'$.
For $\sin\theta=-\tfrac23$, let $B=\sin^{-1}(\tfrac23)$. Sine is negative in Q3 and Q4, so $\theta=180^{\circ}+B,360^{\circ}-B$, giving $221^{\circ}49',318^{\circ}11'$.
All angles are rounded to the nearest minute.

$$\begin{align*}4\sin^3\theta-3\sin\theta&=0\\\sin\theta(4\sin^2\theta-3)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\sin\theta=0$ or $\sin^2\theta=\tfrac34$.
For $\sin\theta=0$, $\theta=0^{\circ},180^{\circ}$.
Otherwise $\sin\theta=\pm\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, with reference angle $60^{\circ}$. Positive sine gives $60^{\circ},120^{\circ}$; negative sine gives $240^{\circ},300^{\circ}$.
Thus $\theta=0^{\circ},60^{\circ},120^{\circ},180^{\circ},240^{\circ},300^{\circ}$. The upper endpoint $360^{\circ}$ is excluded.

content.prompt: Solve $4\cos^2\theta+2\sin\theta=3$ for $0\leq\theta<360^\circ$ to the nearest degree.

answer.worked:
Using $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}4(1-\sin^2\theta)+2\sin\theta&=3\\4-4\sin^2\theta+2\sin\theta&=3\\4\sin^2\theta-2\sin\theta-1&=0\\\sin\theta&=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{(-2)^2-4(4)(-1)}}{8}\\\sin\theta&=\frac{1\pm\sqrt5}{4}\end{align*}$$
For $\sin\theta=\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{4}>0$, use quadrants 1 and 2:
$$\begin{align*}A&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1+\sqrt5}{4}\right)\\A&=54^\circ\\\theta&=54^\circ\text{ or }180^\circ-54^\circ\\\theta&=54^\circ\text{ or }126^\circ\end{align*}$$
For $\sin\theta=\dfrac{1-\sqrt5}{4}<0$, use the positive ratio for the reference angle and quadrants 3 and 4:
$$\begin{align*}A&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4}\right)\\A&=18^\circ\\\theta&=180^\circ+18^\circ\text{ or }360^\circ-18^\circ\\\theta&=198^\circ\text{ or }342^\circ\end{align*}$$
To the nearest degree, $\theta=54^\circ,126^\circ,198^\circ,342^\circ$.

content.prompt: Consider the diagram.

spec.description: Triangle ABC with D on AC and segment BD. Positive axes are arrowed and labelled; no grid, ticks, equality marks or right-angle marker. The acute inclination at A is labelled theta.
spec.mathematics: A=(1,0), B=(0,8), C=(7,4), D=(4,2). AC has gradient 2/3. D is plotted but its coordinates are not supplied to students.
spec.answerVisibility: All source givens and labels visible; derived coordinates and measurements omitted.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the gradient of line $AC$ and hence determine $\theta$, correct to the nearest degree.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the coordinates of the midpoint $D$ of $AC$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}m_{BD}&=\frac{2-8}{4-0}\\m_{BD}&=-\frac32\\m_{AC}m_{BD}&=\frac23\left(-\frac32\right)\\m_{AC}m_{BD}&=-1.\end{align*}$$
The gradients have product $-1$, so $AC\perp BD$.
$BD$ is perpendicular to $AC$ and passes through its midpoint, so $BD$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AC$. Therefore $BA=BC$, and triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.

children.label: f
children.prompt: Find the area of this triangle.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}AC&=\sqrt{(7-1)^2+(4-0)^2}\\AC&=\sqrt{52}\\BD&=\sqrt{(4-0)^2+(2-8)^2}\\BD&=\sqrt{52}.\end{align*}$$
Since $BD\perp AC$, $BD$ is the perpendicular height.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Area}&=\frac12\times AC\times BD\\\text{Area}&=\frac12\times\sqrt{52}\times\sqrt{52}\\\text{Area}&=26\text{ square units}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: g
children.prompt: Write the coordinates of a point $E$ such that $ABCE$ is a rhombus.

answer.worked:
The diagonals $AC$ and $BE$ must bisect each other at $D(4,2)$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{0+x_E}{2}&=4\\x_E&=8\\\frac{8+y_E}{2}&=2\\y_E&=-4.\end{align*}$$
Thus $E=(8,-4)$. The diagonals bisect each other and are perpendicular, so $ABCE$ is a rhombus.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{\sin\theta}{200}&=\frac{\sin25^\circ}{100}\\
\sin\theta&=2\sin25^\circ
\end{align*}$$
The acute possibility is $\alpha=\sin^{-1}(2\sin25^\circ)$. The other possibility is $180^\circ-\alpha$.

Both are valid: $\alpha>25^\circ$, so $(180^\circ-\alpha)+25^\circ<180^\circ$; also $\alpha+25^\circ<180^\circ$.

To the nearest degree, $\theta=58^\circ$ or $122^\circ$.

The supplementary possibility $180^\circ-\alpha$ is obtuse. Together with $130^\circ$, it exceeds $180^\circ$, so it is invalid. The acute possibility satisfies $\alpha+130^\circ<180^\circ$.

To the nearest degree, $\theta=21^\circ$ only.

answer.worked:

content.prompt:
Two triangles are shown, with sides 6 cm and 4 cm. The angle opposite the 4 cm side is $36^\circ$.

Find, in each case, the angle opposite the 6 cm side, correct to the nearest degree.

spec.description: Two triangles side by side with horizontal bases and 36° at their lower-right vertices. The left triangle has an obtuse lower-left angle; the right has an acute lower-left angle. Ordinary source strokes are rendered black.

answer.worked:
Let $\theta$ be the angle opposite the 6 cm side.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{\sin\theta}{6}&=\frac{\sin36^\circ}{4}\\\sin\theta&=\frac{6\sin36^\circ}{4}.\end{align*}$$
The acute possibility is
$$\begin{align*}\theta_1&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{6\sin36^\circ}{4}\right)\\\theta_1&\approx61.8454^\circ.\end{align*}$$
The obtuse possibility is
$$\begin{align*}\theta_2&=180^\circ-\theta_1\\\theta_2&\approx118.1546^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Both are valid because $36^\circ+118.1546^\circ<180^\circ$.

The left triangle has the obtuse angle, so its required angle is $118^\circ$. The right triangle has the acute angle, so its required angle is $62^\circ$, to the nearest degree.

content.prompt: Find all possible lengths of the third side of triangle $ABC$ given $AB=6.2\text{ cm}$, $\angle ABC=35^\circ$ and $AC=4.1\text{ cm}$. Answer to 1 d.p.

answer.worked:
By the sine rule,
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{\sin C}{6.2}&=\frac{\sin35^\circ}{4.1}\\\sin C&=\frac{6.2\sin35^\circ}{4.1}.\end{aligned}$$
Let $\alpha=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{6.2\sin35^\circ}{4.1}\right)$. Then $C=\alpha$ or $180^\circ-\alpha$. Both are valid because $35^\circ+C<180^\circ$ in each case.

For $C=\alpha$,
$$\begin{aligned}A&=180^\circ-35^\circ-\alpha\\BC&=\frac{4.1\sin(145^\circ-\alpha)}{\sin35^\circ}\\BC&\approx7.1\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}$$
For $C=180^\circ-\alpha$,
$$\begin{aligned}A&=180^\circ-35^\circ-(180^\circ-\alpha)\\A&=\alpha-35^\circ\\BC&=\frac{4.1\sin(\alpha-35^\circ)}{\sin35^\circ}\\BC&\approx3.0\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}$$
The third side is $7.1\text{ cm}$ or $3.0\text{ cm}$, to 1 decimal place.

content.prompt: Find the exact value of the area of $\triangle KLM$ and hence find the exact value of $x$.

spec.description: Unshaded triangle KLM with horizontal base LM. N lies between K and M, and LN divides the angle at L into two labelled 30-degree angles. Ordinary lines and labels use black.
spec.mathematics: KL=3, LM=6, angle KLN=30 degrees, angle NLM=30 degrees, LN=x. Coordinates are derived from these relationships; no coordinate values or additional measurements are printed.
spec.answerVisibility: All edges, names, angle labels and supplied lengths are permanent question givens. The numerical value of x is absent.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}
\angle KLM&=30^{\circ}+30^{\circ}\\
&=60^{\circ}\\
\operatorname{Area}(\triangle KLM)&=\frac12(3)(6)\sin60^{\circ}\\
&=\frac{9\sqrt3}{2}.
\end{aligned}$$
Since $N$ lies on $KM$, the two smaller triangle areas add to the whole triangle area.
$$\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Area}(\triangle KLN)+\operatorname{Area}(\triangle NLM)&=\operatorname{Area}(\triangle KLM)\\
\frac12(3)x\sin30^{\circ}+\frac12(6)x\sin30^{\circ}&=\frac{9\sqrt3}{2}\\
\frac34x+\frac32x&=\frac{9\sqrt3}{2}\\
\frac{9x}{4}&=\frac{9\sqrt3}{2}\\
x&=2\sqrt3.
\end{aligned}$$

entries.description:
We express trigonometric ratios for obtuse angles θ according to its acute reference angle A:
sin θ = sin A
cos θ = −cos A
tan θ = −tan A

You will learn more about the inverse trigonometric functions in the Year 12 Advanced course.

1. Find the acute reference angle using the inverse function on the calculator.

3. Calculate θ for each quadrant.
For now, you will only be asked to solve equations where 0 ≤ θ < 360°

entries.description:
Investigation Gradient and Tan
Consider a line through the origin. Choose any point (x, y) on the line.
The gradient is: m = rise/run = [response]
Construct a right-angled triangle, the ratio tan θ = opp/adj = [response]
Therefore, m = tan θ.
We can extend this relationship to all lines, not just ones through the origin, since the gradient and angle of inclination does not change based on the location of the line.

entries.description:
Finding the Angle of Inclination from the Gradient
θ = tan⁻¹(m)
If the calculator returns a negative angle, add 180° to the result.
tan⁻¹( ) function always returns angles in the range −90° < θ < 90°.
Angle of inclination of a line is an angle 0 ≤ θ < 180°.
We add 180° to the result because tan θ = tan(180° + θ).

entries.description:
If the question doesn’t tell you whether a triangle has an acute or obtuse angle:
1. Use sine rule to find the unknown acute angle θ.
2. Find the obtuse angle θ′ = 180° − θ.
3. Add θ′ to the given angle. If the sum > 180°, it is not a valid possibility (angle sum of triangle cannot exceed 180°).
Warning: Diagrams are never drawn to scale. In an exam, if you see a sine rule question worth 3 marks or more, it is likely the ambiguous case and marks will be awarded for justifying all possible answers.
